name: Kohistani Shina
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Schmidt, Ruth Laila & Vijay Kumar Kaul. 2008. A comparative analysis of Shina and Kashmiri vocabularies. Acta Orientalia 69: 231-302 (open access, doi 10.5617/ao.7372). Kohistani (Palas) word list supplied by Muhammad Manzar Zarin and Razwal Kohistani (p. 232 fn. 2).
catalog_locator: p. 234 main text and footnote 5; p. 244 footnote 17.
catalog_quote: The pitch accent is shown in the Gilgiti, Kohistani, Guresi, Astori and Drasi entries. [fn. 5] Every Shina word contains one accented syllable. In short syllables, the accent is realized as a high pitch and is shown as an acute accent over the vowel (áẓo 'rain'). The accent need not be written on short monosyllables. Long syllables, written with double vowels, normally carry the word accent. Except in Brokskat, long vowels may have a high falling pitch, shown as an acute accent on the first vowel, or mora (táaro 'star'); or a low rising pitch, shown as an acute accent on the second vowel or mora (baál 'child'). Unaccented long vowels have been documented for Kohistani, but not for the remaining dialects.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (72 pp., scanned text) and the page render. Footnote 5 on p. 234 (p. 4) reads exactly as quoted: 'Every Shina word contains one accented syllable. In short syllables, the accent is realized as a high pitch and is shown as an acute accent over the vowel (áẓo 'rain'). The accent need not be written on short monosyllables. Long syllables, written with double vowels, normally carry the word accent. Except in Brokskat, long vowels may have a high falling pitch, shown as an acute accent on the first vowel, or mora (táaro 'star'); or a low rising pitch, shown as an acute accent on the second vowel or mora (baál 'child'). Unaccented long vowels have been documented for Kohistani, but not for…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One accent per word, realised as high pitch; its position is not given by a positional rule but is a property of the word (lexical, mora-based): on a short syllable the accented vowel is high, on a long vowel the accent sits on either the first mora (high falling pitch) or the second mora (low rising pitch). Long (double-vowel) syllables normally attract the accent, so the system is weight-sensitive in tendency only; Kohistani in particular has unaccented long vowels. Main text p. 234 calls it 'the pitch accent'. Secondary analyses of the same Kohistani data (Baart c.2003 after Schmidt & Kohistani 1998: 125-134; Liljegren 2013 after Schmidt & Kohistani 2008: 24-28) describe it as stress assigned lexically to one mora with a H tone linked to that mora.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent need not be written on short monosyllables; Brokskat lacks the falling/rising contrast (stress marked instead); unaccented long vowels occur in Kohistani but not the other dialects. p. 244 fn. 17: accent on the second mora 'in most cases results from secondary lengthening following the reduction of ancient consonant clusters' (tapta- > tatta > taáto 'hot'), while an OIA long vowel gives accent on the first mora (bhrātr- > ẓáa). The 2008 grammar's TOC lists 'Phonologically conditioned accent shift in nouns' (p. 49) and root- vs stem-accented verb classes (pp. 136, 154), i.e. morphologically governed accent placement in inflection.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in a 280-item comparative wordlist; the note is a transcription convention stated for all six Shina dialects listed (Gilgiti, Kohistani, Guresi, Astori, Drasi, with Brokskat excepted), and the Kohistani entries carry the accent marks. It is not a Kohistani-specific phonology section; that section is Schmidt & Kohistani 2008 §2.2.4 pp. 24-28 (unopened).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is a pan-Shina transcription note by Schmidt (the author of the Kohistani grammar) in a comparative wordlist paper; it explicitly covers the Kohistani list, which was supplied by Palas speakers (M. M. Zarin, Razwal Kohistani), i.e. the Palas/Indus Kohistan variety = kohi1248 proper, and it adds one Kohistani-specific remark (unaccented long vowels). It is not a Kohistani-only phonology section; the dedicated description is Schmidt & Kohistani 2008 §2.2.4 (unopened). Glottolog's Ganai 2014 'Kohistani' (Languages of Jammu and Kashmir) may not be this language.

tone_statements.quote: Varieties of Shina contrast falling and rising accent in bimoraic stressed syllables with long vowels. In this paper, I mark falling tone with an acute accent (H) on the first part of a long vowel (e.g. [áa]) and rising with an acute accent (H) on the second part (e.g. [aá]) ... Two minimal pairs are provided in (1): (1) a. [báak] ‘push’ [baák] ‘agreement’ b. [móos] ‘month’ [moós] ‘flesh’ ... Based on the available data, I propose that both the falling and the rising accent in Kohistani Shina derive from a difference in the alignment of an intonational LH* pitch accent, which is followed by a phrase-final low boundary tone.

sources.note: Secondary/typological. Kohistani Shina coded from 'Schmidt and Kohistani 2008; own data'. §4.8 Tones: HK Indo-Aryan tone is always a word-level feature; Baart's (2014) taxonomy: 2-way contrast 'Shina-type tone', 'often described as pitch accent', the most common type, with Gilgiti Shina as typical representative; Kalami-type (Kalkoti) is the complex type.

sources.citation: Liljegren, Henrik. 2013. Notes on Kalkoti: A Shina language with strong Kohistani influences. Linguistic Discovery 11(1). doi:10.1349/PS1.1537-0852.A.423
sources.note: Secondary, on Kalkoti: 'a relatively simple tonal accent system, much like that found in other Shina varieties (Liljegren 2008, 74-77.. Radloff 1999, 57-107; Schmidt and Kohistani 2008, 24-28). In such a system, one high tone is associated with a single mora.' Also cites Kohistani Shina vowel system from Schmidt & Kohistani 2008: 15-18 and Kohistani forms súuri 'sun', táaro 'star', ac̣híi 'eye'.

sources.citation: Baart, Joan L. G. c.2003. Tonal features in languages of northern Pakistan. Ms. (SIL/Kalam Cultural Society).
sources.note: Secondary. pp. 4, 9-10: Shina (Gilgit, Kohistan, Kashmir) has two surface tones, high-falling vs low-rising, contrastive only on long vowels; 'according to the analysis of several linguists (see Schmidt & Kohistani 1998: 125-134, Radloff 1999: 83-88..)' underlying forms have no tone: 'stress applies to the mora. Stress is assigned to one of the moras of the word', H tone links to the stressed mora, L elsewhere.

Says Shina is tonal with tone only on long vowels (rising vs falling), but sources this to a Gilgit-oriented orthography pamphlet (Shakeel 2008) and Gilgiti dictionaries, not to a Kohistani description; nothing on stress placement.
